igcse-0580-indices-ii-products-quotients.description: Group powers by their letter base, calculate the coefficient separately and simplify algebraic quotients.

sections.title: How do I join powers of the same letter?
sections.label: Products and an unwritten index
sections.intro: A power counts repeated factors. In a product of powers of the same letter, all the copies of that letter belong to one group.

blocks.html: Use \(x^m x^n=x^{m+n}\). A letter on its own contributes one factor, so \(x=x^1\). Multiply the ordinary numerical coefficients separately.

blocks.title: Join matching groups of factors
blocks.prompt: Write \(x^{3}\times x^{4}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).
blocks.hint: Add the counts of matching factors when the powers are multiplied.
blocks.solution:
The base is \(x\) in both factors. Count all the copies of this base.

Add the indices using \(3+4=7\).

The result is \(x^{7}\), so \(p=7\).

blocks.html: Adding two terms is different from multiplying their factors. For example, \(x^2+x^2=2x^2\). The expression \(x^2x^2\) is \(x^4\).

blocks.title: Use the unwritten index of one
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(4x\times 3x^{3}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
blocks.hint: A letter written without a visible index has index one.
blocks.solution:
The first \(x\) contributes one factor. The second term contributes \(3\) factors of \(x\).

Multiply the number parts to get \(12\). Add the two index values separately.

The simplified expression is \(12x^{4}\). In the requested form, \(c=12\), \(p=4\).

blocks.html: Write a short line showing the coefficient multiplication and the index addition independently.

sections.title: What does the denominator remove?
sections.label: Subtract matching denominator indices
sections.intro: A common nonzero factor can be cancelled from the top and bottom of a fraction. Cross off one pair at a time if a quotient is new to you.

blocks.html: For \(x\ne0\), use \(\frac{x^m}{x^n}=x^{m-n}\). Subtract the denominator index from the numerator index. Divide the coefficients as a separate calculation.

figure.alt: Matching pairs of factors in a numerator and denominator are crossed out. A numerator factor remains.
figure.caption: The lines join equal nonzero factors. Only uncancelled factors contribute to the quotient.

blocks.title: Cancel the matching factors in a quotient
blocks.prompt: For \(x\ne0\), Write \(\frac{x^{10}}{x^{3}}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).
blocks.hint: Subtract the denominator's index from the numerator's index.
blocks.solution:
Because \(x\ne 0\), cancel one matching factor at a time.

The number of factors remaining above the bar is \(10-3=7\).

The result is \(x^{7}\), so \(p=7\).

blocks.html: The order of subtraction follows the fraction. Reversing top and bottom changes the resulting power.

blocks.title: Divide coefficients and powers separately
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{12x^{8}}{3x^{3}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
blocks.hint: Divide the number parts and subtract the indices for the same letter.
blocks.solution:
The coefficient of the quotient is \(\frac{12}{3}=4\).

The letters give index \(8-3=5\).

The simplified expression is \(4x^{5}\). In the requested form, \(c=4\), \(p=5\).

blocks.html: The simplification is valid wherever the original quotient is defined. Keep the condition that its denominator is nonzero.

sections.title: How do I handle more than one letter?
sections.label: Keep a group for each base
sections.intro: In an expression built from products or quotients, sort the factors into their numerical parts and one group per letter.

blocks.html: In \(5x^3y\cdot 2xy^4\), group the two coefficient factors, the copies of \(x\) and the copies of \(y\). The result is \(10x^4y^5\).

blocks.title: Group two different letter bases
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(3x^{4}y^{3}\times 4x^{3}y\) as \(cx^{p}y^{q}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\).
blocks.hint: Keep the counts for each letter in a separate group.
blocks.solution:
Group the counts for \(x\) and \(y\) separately. The lone \(y\) contributes one factor.

The numerical product is \(12\). The indices are \(4+3\) and \(3+1\).

The simplified expression is \(12x^{7}y^{4}\). In the requested form, \(c=12\), \(p=7\), \(q=4\).

blocks.html: Do not add the indices of different bases. The powers of \(x\) provide no extra factors of \(y\).

blocks.title: Combine a product and a quotient
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{3x^{5}y\times 4xy^{3}}{3x^{2}y}\) as \(cx^{p}y^{q}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\).
blocks.hint: Simplify the product in the numerator before dividing.
blocks.solution:
In the numerator the index of \(x\) is \(5+1\) and the index of \(y\) is \(1+3\).

Now subtract the denominator's indices \(2\) and \(1\). The common coefficient \(3\) cancels.

The simplified expression is \(4x^{4}y^{3}\). In the requested form, \(c=4\), \(p=4\), \(q=3\).

blocks.html: When the numerator has several factors, simplify the numerator before dividing or use a separate index calculation for each letter.

examples.title: Join matching groups of factors
examples.question: Write \(x^{2}\times x^{3}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).
solution: The base is \(x\) in both factors. Count all the copies of this base.
Add the indices using \(2+3=5\).
The result is \(x^{5}\), so \(p=5\).

examples.title: Use the unwritten index of one
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(3x\times 2x^{2}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
solution: The first \(x\) contributes one factor. The second term contributes \(2\) factors of \(x\).
Multiply the number parts to get \(6\). Add the two index values separately.
The simplified expression is \(6x^{3}\). In the requested form, \(c=6\), \(p=3\).

examples.title: Cancel the matching factors in a quotient
examples.question: For \(x\ne0\), Write \(\frac{x^{9}}{x^{2}}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).
solution: Because \(x\ne 0\), cancel one matching factor at a time.
The number of factors remaining above the bar is \(9-2=7\).
The result is \(x^{7}\), so \(p=7\).

examples.title: Divide coefficients and powers separately
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{6x^{7}}{2x^{2}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
solution: The coefficient of the quotient is \(\frac{6}{2}=3\).
The letters give index \(7-2=5\).
The simplified expression is \(3x^{5}\). In the requested form, \(c=3\), \(p=5\).

examples.title: Group two different letter bases
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(2x^{3}y^{2}\times 3x^{2}y\) as \(cx^{p}y^{q}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\).
solution: Group the counts for \(x\) and \(y\) separately. The lone \(y\) contributes one factor.
The numerical product is \(6\). The indices are \(3+2\) and \(2+1\).
The simplified expression is \(6x^{5}y^{3}\). In the requested form, \(c=6\), \(p=5\), \(q=3\).

examples.title: Combine a product and a quotient
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{2x^{4}y\times 3xy^{2}}{2x^{2}y}\) as \(cx^{p}y^{q}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\).
solution: In the numerator the index of \(x\) is \(4+1\) and the index of \(y\) is \(1+2\).
Now subtract the denominator's indices \(2\) and \(1\). The common coefficient \(2\) cancels.
The simplified expression is \(3x^{3}y^{2}\). In the requested form, \(c=3\), \(p=3\), \(q=2\).

extraPractice.title: Join matching groups of factors
extraPractice.prompt: Write \(x^{4}\times x^{5}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).
extraPractice.hint: Add the counts of matching factors when the powers are multiplied.
extraPractice.solution:
The base is \(x\) in both factors. Count all the copies of this base.

Add the indices using \(4+5=9\).

The result is \(x^{9}\), so \(p=9\).

extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(5x\times 4x^{4}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
extraPractice.hint: A letter written without a visible index has index one.
extraPractice.solution:
The first \(x\) contributes one factor. The second term contributes \(4\) factors of \(x\).

Multiply the number parts to get \(20\). Add the two index values separately.

The simplified expression is \(20x^{5}\). In the requested form, \(c=20\), \(p=5\).

extraPractice.title: Cancel the matching factors in a quotient
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x\ne0\), Write \(\frac{x^{11}}{x^{4}}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).
extraPractice.hint: Subtract the denominator's index from the numerator's index.
extraPractice.solution:
Because \(x\ne 0\), cancel one matching factor at a time.

The result is \(x^{7}\), so \(p=7\).

extraPractice.title: Divide coefficients and powers separately
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{20x^{9}}{4x^{4}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
extraPractice.hint: Divide the number parts and subtract the indices for the same letter.
extraPractice.solution:
The coefficient of the quotient is \(\frac{20}{4}=5\).

The letters give index \(9-4=5\).

The simplified expression is \(5x^{5}\). In the requested form, \(c=5\), \(p=5\).

extraPractice.title: Group two different letter bases
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(4x^{5}y^{4}\times 5x^{4}y\) as \(cx^{p}y^{q}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\).
extraPractice.hint: Keep the counts for each letter in a separate group.
extraPractice.solution:
Group the counts for \(x\) and \(y\) separately. The lone \(y\) contributes one factor.

The numerical product is \(20\). The indices are \(5+4\) and \(4+1\).

The simplified expression is \(20x^{9}y^{5}\). In the requested form, \(c=20\), \(p=9\), \(q=5\).

extraPractice.title: Combine a product and a quotient
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{4x^{6}y\times 5xy^{4}}{4x^{2}y}\) as \(cx^{p}y^{q}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\).
extraPractice.hint: Simplify the product in the numerator before dividing.
extraPractice.solution:
In the numerator the index of \(x\) is \(6+1\) and the index of \(y\) is \(1+4\).

Now subtract the denominator's indices \(2\) and \(1\). The common coefficient \(4\) cancels.

The simplified expression is \(5x^{5}y^{4}\). In the requested form, \(c=5\), \(p=5\), \(q=4\).

glossary.definition: The number or symbol being repeatedly multiplied.
The exponent written above and to the right of a base.
The number multiplying a letter expression.
The result of dividing.
Divide the numerator and denominator by the same nonzero factor.

revision.body:
Products and an unwritten index

Use \(x^m x^n=x^{m+n}\). A letter on its own contributes one factor, so \(x=x^1\). Multiply the ordinary numerical coefficients separately.

Subtract matching denominator indices

For \(x e0\), use \( rac{x^m}{x^n}=x^{m-n}\). Subtract the denominator index from the numerator index. Divide the coefficients as a separate calculation.

Keep a group for each base

In \(5x^3y\cdot 2xy^4\), group the two coefficient factors, the copies of \(x\) and the copies of \(y\). The result is \(10x^4y^5\).

Example

\( rac{18x^8}{6x^3}=3x^5\) for \(x e0\). Divide 18 by 6 and subtract 3 from 8.

Check yourself

  • Simplify \(4a^3b^2\cdot 3a^2b\).
  • Simplify \( rac{45m^9}{9m^3}\) for \(m e0\).

Answers \(12a^5b^3\) and \(5m^6\).
revision.checks:
• Adding two terms is different from multiplying their factors. For example, \(x^2+x^2=2x^2\). The expression \(x^2x^2\) is \(x^4\).
  • The order of subtraction follows the fraction. Reversing top and bottom changes the resulting power.
  • Do not add the indices of different bases. The powers of \(x\) provide no extra factors of \(y\).
revision.examTip: When the numerator has several factors, simplify the numerator before dividing or use a separate index calculation for each letter.

igcse-0580-indices-ii-zero-negative-powe.description: Apply an outer power to an entire bracket and use reciprocals to write positive indices.

sections.title: What exactly does an outside index act on?
sections.label: Repeat the complete bracket
sections.intro: A whole bracket raised to a power behaves as one base. Read the brackets before deciding what the outside index applies to.

blocks.html: Use \((cx^m)^n=c^n x^{mn}\). The outer power acts on the coefficient as well as the letter. If the bracket contains a quotient, simplify the quotient first when possible.

figure.alt: An outer power is connected by arrows to both the coefficient and the letter factor inside a bracket.
figure.caption: Both factors are inside the repeated group. Apply the exponent to each one.

blocks.title: Raise every factor inside the brackets
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(3x^{4}\right)^{3}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
blocks.hint: The outside index acts on the number and on the letter.
blocks.solution:
Repeat the entire product inside the brackets \(3\) times.

The numerical factor becomes \(3^{3}=27\). The two powers on the letter combine to \(4\times 3=12\).

The simplified expression is \(27x^{12}\). In the requested form, \(c=27\), \(p=12\).

blocks.html: In \((4x^2)^3\), the multiplier becomes \(4^3\). It is easy to cube only the letter and accidentally retain 4.

blocks.title: Apply a zero index to a whole base
blocks.prompt: Find the value of \(\left(4x^{3}\right)^{0}\) for \(x\ne0\).
blocks.hint: Identify the whole base. Its zero power has value one.
blocks.solution:
The entire base is \(4x^{3}\). It is nonzero because \(x\ne0\).

Any nonzero base raised to the power zero has value 1.

blocks.html: As a check, expand a small outer power into repeated groups before simplifying.

sections.title: Why does a zero exponent give one?
sections.label: Cancel the same nonzero powers
sections.intro: Dividing a nonzero power by itself gives one. The quotient law also gives the difference of two identical indices, which is zero.

blocks.html: For a nonzero base \(A\), \(A^0=1\). If a bracket has exponent zero, first identify the whole bracket as the base.

blocks.title: Simplify a quotient before raising it
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(\frac{3x^{4}}{3x}\right)^{4}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
blocks.hint: You can simplify the nonzero quotient first, then apply the outside power.
blocks.solution:
Inside the bracket the coefficients cancel. The quotient of letters becomes \(x^{3}\).

Then apply the outside power. The indices multiply to \(3\times 4=12\).

The simplified expression is \(x^{12}\). In the requested form, \(c=1\), \(p=12\).

blocks.html: A zero exponent does not make the expression zero. If the base is zero, the rule does not apply.

blocks.title: Move only the factor with a negative index
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(3x^{-3}\) as \(\frac{c}{x^{p}}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\). Use positive indices in the final expression.
blocks.hint: The coefficient is not part of a negative power unless it is inside its brackets.
blocks.solution:
The minus sign applies only to the index of \(x\).

Use \(x^{-3}=\frac{1}{x^{3}}\) and keep the original coefficient \(3\).

The simplified expression is \(\frac{3}{x^{3}}\). In the requested form, \(c=3\), \(p=3\).

blocks.html: Name the original nonzero base when explaining why a zero power equals one.

sections.title: Which factor moves when the exponent is negative?
sections.label: Use a reciprocal and retain scope
sections.intro: A negative exponent makes a reciprocal of the matching positive power. The scope may be one letter or a whole bracket.

blocks.html: Compare \(4x^{-3}=\frac{4}{x^3}\) and \((4x^3)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4x^3}\). For a quotient, subtract the indices first and then convert any remaining negative power to a reciprocal.

blocks.title: Take the reciprocal of a powered bracket
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(3x^{3}\right)^{-2}\) as \(\frac{c}{x^{p}}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\). Use positive indices in the final expression.
blocks.hint: Take the reciprocal of the whole power, including the constant inside the bracket.
blocks.solution:
First write the reciprocal of the square of the whole bracket.

The square in the denominator is \(9x^{6}\). The coefficient in the requested template is \(\frac{1}{9}\).

The simplified expression is \(\frac{1}{9x^{6}}\). In the requested form, \(c=\frac{1}{9}\), \(p=6\).

blocks.html: Moving a negative-index factor through the fraction bar changes its exponent sign. It does not change the sign of the factor's coefficient.

blocks.title: Write a quotient using positive indices
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{4x^{3}y^{-3}}{3x^{6}y}\) as \(\frac{c}{x^{p}y^{q}}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\). Use positive indices in the final expression.
blocks.hint: Work with signed indices first. Move a whole factor across the bar when its final index is negative.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the denominator's indices to get \(-3\) for \(x\) and \(-4\) for \(y\).

Move both letter factors into the denominator with positive indices. Keep the reduced numerical factor \(\frac{4}{3}\).

The simplified expression is \(\frac{4}{3x^{3}y^{4}}\). In the requested form, \(c=\frac{4}{3}\), \(p=3\), \(q=4\).

blocks.html: Use a separate line for the signed exponents before writing the final expression with positive exponents.

examples.title: Raise every factor inside the brackets
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(2x^{3}\right)^{2}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
solution: Repeat the entire product inside the brackets \(2\) times.
The numerical factor becomes \(2^{2}=4\). The two powers on the letter combine to \(3\times 2=6\).
The simplified expression is \(4x^{6}\). In the requested form, \(c=4\), \(p=6\).

examples.title: Apply a zero index to a whole base
examples.question: Find the value of \(\left(3x^{2}\right)^{0}\) for \(x\ne0\).
solution: The entire base is \(3x^{2}\). It is nonzero because \(x\ne0\).
Any nonzero base raised to the power zero has value 1.

examples.title: Simplify a quotient before raising it
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(\frac{2x^{3}}{2x}\right)^{3}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
solution: Inside the bracket the coefficients cancel. The quotient of letters becomes \(x^{2}\).
Then apply the outside power. The indices multiply to \(2\times 3=6\).
The simplified expression is \(x^{6}\). In the requested form, \(c=1\), \(p=6\).

examples.title: Move only the factor with a negative index
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(2x^{-2}\) as \(\frac{c}{x^{p}}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\). Use positive indices in the final expression.
solution: The minus sign applies only to the index of \(x\).
Use \(x^{-2}=\frac{1}{x^{2}}\) and keep the original coefficient \(2\).
The simplified expression is \(\frac{2}{x^{2}}\). In the requested form, \(c=2\), \(p=2\).

examples.title: Take the reciprocal of a powered bracket
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(2x^{2}\right)^{-2}\) as \(\frac{c}{x^{p}}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\). Use positive indices in the final expression.
solution: First write the reciprocal of the square of the whole bracket.
The square in the denominator is \(4x^{4}\). The coefficient in the requested template is \(\frac{1}{4}\).
The simplified expression is \(\frac{1}{4x^{4}}\). In the requested form, \(c=\frac{1}{4}\), \(p=4\).

examples.title: Write a quotient using positive indices
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{3x^{2}y^{-2}}{2x^{5}y}\) as \(\frac{c}{x^{p}y^{q}}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\). Use positive indices in the final expression.
solution: Subtract the denominator's indices to get \(-3\) for \(x\) and \(-3\) for \(y\).
Move both letter factors into the denominator with positive indices. Keep the reduced numerical factor \(\frac{3}{2}\).
The simplified expression is \(\frac{3}{2x^{3}y^{3}}\). In the requested form, \(c=\frac{3}{2}\), \(p=3\), \(q=3\).

extraPractice.title: Raise every factor inside the brackets
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(4x^{5}\right)^{2}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
extraPractice.hint: The outside index acts on the number and on the letter.
extraPractice.solution:
Repeat the entire product inside the brackets \(2\) times.

The numerical factor becomes \(4^{2}=16\). The two powers on the letter combine to \(5\times 2=10\).

The simplified expression is \(16x^{10}\). In the requested form, \(c=16\), \(p=10\).

extraPractice.prompt: Find the value of \(\left(5x^{4}\right)^{0}\) for \(x\ne0\).
extraPractice.hint: Identify the whole base. Its zero power has value one.
extraPractice.solution:
The entire base is \(5x^{4}\). It is nonzero because \(x\ne0\).

Any nonzero base raised to the power zero has value 1.

extraPractice.title: Simplify a quotient before raising it
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(\frac{4x^{5}}{4x}\right)^{5}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
extraPractice.hint: You can simplify the nonzero quotient first, then apply the outside power.
extraPractice.solution:
Inside the bracket the coefficients cancel. The quotient of letters becomes \(x^{4}\).

Then apply the outside power. The indices multiply to \(4\times 5=20\).

The simplified expression is \(x^{20}\). In the requested form, \(c=1\), \(p=20\).

extraPractice.title: Move only the factor with a negative index
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(4x^{-4}\) as \(\frac{c}{x^{p}}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\). Use positive indices in the final expression.
extraPractice.hint: The coefficient is not part of a negative power unless it is inside its brackets.
extraPractice.solution:
The minus sign applies only to the index of \(x\).

Use \(x^{-4}=\frac{1}{x^{4}}\) and keep the original coefficient \(4\).

The simplified expression is \(\frac{4}{x^{4}}\). In the requested form, \(c=4\), \(p=4\).

extraPractice.title: Take the reciprocal of a powered bracket
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(4x^{4}\right)^{-2}\) as \(\frac{c}{x^{p}}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\). Use positive indices in the final expression.
extraPractice.hint: Take the reciprocal of the whole power, including the constant inside the bracket.
extraPractice.solution:
First write the reciprocal of the square of the whole bracket.

The square in the denominator is \(16x^{8}\). The coefficient in the requested template is \(\frac{1}{16}\).

The simplified expression is \(\frac{1}{16x^{8}}\). In the requested form, \(c=\frac{1}{16}\), \(p=8\).

extraPractice.title: Write a quotient using positive indices
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{5x^{4}y^{-4}}{4x^{7}y}\) as \(\frac{c}{x^{p}y^{q}}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\). Use positive indices in the final expression.
extraPractice.hint: Work with signed indices first. Move a whole factor across the bar when its final index is negative.
extraPractice.solution:
Subtract the denominator's indices to get \(-3\) for \(x\) and \(-5\) for \(y\).

Move both letter factors into the denominator with positive indices. Keep the reduced numerical factor \(\frac{5}{4}\).

The simplified expression is \(\frac{5}{4x^{3}y^{5}}\). In the requested form, \(c=\frac{5}{4}\), \(p=3\), \(q=5\).

One divided by a nonzero number or expression.
Exponents that are greater than zero.
An exponent of zero, giving one for a nonzero base.
The factors that an operation applies to.

revision.body:
Repeat the complete bracket

Use \((cx^m)^n=c^n x^{mn}\). The outer power acts on the coefficient as well as the letter. If the bracket contains a quotient, simplify the quotient first when possible.

Cancel the same nonzero powers

For a nonzero base \(A\), \(A^0=1\). If a bracket has exponent zero, first identify the whole bracket as the base.

Use a reciprocal and retain scope

Compare \(4x^{-3}=\frac{4}{x^3}\) and \((4x^3)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4x^3}\). For a quotient, subtract the indices first and then convert any remaining negative power to a reciprocal.

Example

\((3x^4)^{-2}=\frac{1}{9x^8}\) for \(x\ne0\). Square the whole bracket and take its reciprocal.

Check yourself

  • Simplify \((5a^3)^2\).
  • Use positive indices for \(7y^{-4}\), where \(y\ne0\).

Answers \(25a^6\) and \(\frac7{y^4}\).

  • A zero exponent does not make the expression zero. If the base is zero, the rule does not apply.
  • Moving a negative-index factor through the fraction bar changes its exponent sign. It does not change the sign of the factor's coefficient.

igcse-0580-indices-ii-direct-index-equat.description: Write both sides as powers of the same base and solve a direct equation for an index.

sections.title: How do I find a shared base?
sections.label: Recognise a whole-number power
sections.intro: Read the known base beside the unknown index. The other side must be expressed as a power of that same base before the indices can be compared.

blocks.html: With base greater than 1, the powers increase as their indices increase. Two equal powers of that fixed base have equal indices. For example, \(2^x=128\) becomes \(2^x=2^7\).

figure.alt: A sequence points from recognising the base to matching indices and checking the value.
figure.caption: Write both sides with the same base before forming the equation in the indices.

blocks.title: Match a base to an integer power
blocks.hint: Rewrite the whole number on the right as a power of the base on the left.
blocks.solution:
Build powers of \(3\) by multiplying by one more copy of the base each time.

Write the right-hand side as \(3^{3}\). Match the two index values.

The solution is \(x=3\).

blocks.html: Dividing the right-hand number by the base once does not find its index. Look for repeated multiplication by the base.

blocks.title: Recognise a zero index
blocks.hint: Find the power that every nonzero base has in common at 1.
blocks.solution:
Write 1 as \(4^{0}\). This is valid because the base is nonzero.

The powers of this base have one index that gives 1. Match it to \(x\).

The solution is \(x=0\).

blocks.html: Write both powers in your working before stating the unknown value.

sections.title: What if the right-hand side is one or a fraction?
sections.label: Match zero and negative powers
sections.intro: A power of a base greater than 1 is one when its index is zero. A positive answer smaller than one comes from a negative index.

blocks.html: Rewrite \(\frac{1}{a^n}\) as \(a^{-n}\). If you see \(a^x=1\), the matching power is \(a^0\), provided \(a>1\).

blocks.title: Match an exact reciprocal power
blocks.hint: Write the denominator as a power, then change the sign of its index.
blocks.solution:
The denominator is \(3^{2}\).

An exact reciprocal of a positive power is \(3^{-2}\). Match its index to \(x\).

The solution is \(x=-2\).

blocks.html: A fraction on the right does not force the unknown index to be a fractional number. An integer such as \(-2\) can give an exact reciprocal.

blocks.title: Solve with an unknown index in a product
blocks.hint: Add the two indices on the left before comparing with the right.
blocks.solution:
The factors on the left have the same base. Their combined index is \(3+x\).

Match indices to obtain \(3+x=4\). Then subtract \(3\).

The solution is \(x=1\).

blocks.html: Write down the index of the denominator first. Then use the reciprocal rule to change its sign.

sections.title: What if a side contains a product or quotient?
sections.label: Combine and solve the resulting index equation
sections.intro: A product or quotient of powers of the same base can be written as a single power. Then it is possible to match the index with the single power on the other side.

blocks.html: Add indices in a product and subtract them in a quotient. After matching bases, solve the equation between the resulting index expressions.

blocks.title: Restore a subtracted index
blocks.hint: Use numerator index minus denominator index.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the denominator index in the quotient, giving \(4^{x-3}\).

Equate the indices and add \(3\) to both sides of \(x-3=5\).

The solution is \(x=8\).

blocks.html: A quotient subtracts the index in its denominator. An index attached to a power is not a numerical multiplier outside it.

blocks.title: Compare powers with a stated letter base
blocks.prompt: Let \(a>1\). Solve \(a^{4}\times a^{x}=a^{9}\).
blocks.hint: The statement about the base lets you equate the two indices.
blocks.solution:
The base \(a\) is the same on both sides. Multiplication gives \(a^{4+x}\).

Since \(a>1\), different indices give different powers. Solve \(4+x=9\).

The solution is \(x=5\).

blocks.html: Substitute the index into the original equation and check the two powers agree.

examples.title: Match a base to an integer power
examples.question: Solve \(2^{x}=8\).
solution: Build powers of \(2\) by multiplying by one more copy of the base each time.
Write the right-hand side as \(2^{3}\). Match the two index values.
The solution is \(x=3\).

examples.title: Recognise a zero index
examples.question: Solve \(3^{x}=1\).
solution: Write 1 as \(3^{0}\). This is valid because the base is nonzero.
The powers of this base have one index that gives 1. Match it to \(x\).
The solution is \(x=0\).

examples.title: Match an exact reciprocal power
examples.question: Solve \(2^{x}=\frac{1}{2}\).
solution: The denominator is \(2^{1}\).
An exact reciprocal of a positive power is \(2^{-1}\). Match its index to \(x\).
The solution is \(x=-1\).

examples.title: Solve with an unknown index in a product
examples.question: Solve \(2^{2}\times 2^{x}=2^{3}\).
solution: The factors on the left have the same base. Their combined index is \(2+x\).
Match indices to obtain \(2+x=3\). Then subtract \(2\).
The solution is \(x=1\).

examples.title: Restore a subtracted index
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{3^{x}}{3^{2}}=3^{4}\).
solution: Subtract the denominator index in the quotient, giving \(3^{x-2}\).
Equate the indices and add \(2\) to both sides of \(x-2=4\).
The solution is \(x=6\).

examples.title: Compare powers with a stated letter base
examples.question: Let \(a>1\). Solve \(a^{3}\times a^{x}=a^{8}\).
solution: The base \(a\) is the same on both sides. Multiplication gives \(a^{3+x}\).
Since \(a>1\), different indices give different powers. Solve \(3+x=8\).
The solution is \(x=5\).

extraPractice.title: Match a base to an integer power
extraPractice.hint: Rewrite the whole number on the right as a power of the base on the left.
extraPractice.solution:
Build powers of \(4\) by multiplying by one more copy of the base each time.

Write the right-hand side as \(4^{3}\). Match the two index values.

The solution is \(x=3\).

extraPractice.title: Recognise a zero index
extraPractice.hint: Find the power that every nonzero base has in common at 1.
extraPractice.solution:
Write 1 as \(5^{0}\). This is valid because the base is nonzero.

The powers of this base have one index that gives 1. Match it to \(x\).

The solution is \(x=0\).

extraPractice.title: Match an exact reciprocal power
extraPractice.hint: Write the denominator as a power, then change the sign of its index.
extraPractice.solution:
The denominator is \(5^{3}\).

An exact reciprocal of a positive power is \(5^{-3}\). Match its index to \(x\).

The solution is \(x=-3\).

extraPractice.title: Solve with an unknown index in a product
extraPractice.hint: Add the two indices on the left before comparing with the right.
extraPractice.solution:
The factors on the left have the same base. Their combined index is \(4+x\).

Match indices to obtain \(4+x=5\). Then subtract \(4\).

The solution is \(x=1\).

extraPractice.title: Restore a subtracted index
extraPractice.hint: Use numerator index minus denominator index.
extraPractice.solution:
Subtract the denominator index in the quotient, giving \(5^{x-4}\).

Equate the indices and add \(4\) to both sides of \(x-4=6\).

The solution is \(x=10\).

extraPractice.title: Compare powers with a stated letter base
extraPractice.hint: The statement about the base lets you equate the two indices.
extraPractice.solution:
The base \(a\) is the same on both sides. Multiplication gives \(a^{5+x}\).

Since \(a>1\), different indices give different powers. Solve \(5+x=10\).

The solution is \(x=5\).

glossary.definition: The value to find.
A base whose value stays the same while its exponent varies.
The base used for both sides of an exponential equation.
Another word for index.
Replace the unknown by a tested value.

revision.body:
Recognise a whole-number power

With base greater than 1, the powers increase as their indices increase. Two equal powers of that fixed base have equal indices. For example, \(2^x=128\) becomes \(2^x=2^7\).

Match zero and negative powers

Rewrite \(\frac{1}{a^n}\) as \(a^{-n}\). If you see \(a^x=1\), the matching power is \(a^0\), provided \(a>1\).

Combine and solve the resulting index equation

Add indices in a product and subtract them in a quotient. After matching bases, solve the equation between the resulting index expressions.

Example

\(6^x=\frac{1}{216}=6^{-3}\) gives \(x=-3\). The denominator is \(6^3\).

Check yourself

  • Solve \(7^x=343\).
  • Solve \(\frac{5^x}{5^4}=5^2\).

Answers \(x=3\) and \(x=6\).
revision.checks:
• Dividing the right-hand number by the base once does not find its index. Look for repeated multiplication by the base.
  • A fraction on the right does not force the unknown index to be a fractional number. An integer such as \(-2\) can give an exact reciprocal.
  • A quotient subtracts the index in its denominator. An index attached to a power is not a numerical multiplier outside it.
revision.examTip: Substitute the index into the original equation and check the two powers agree.

igcse-0580-indices-ii-algebraic-fraction.description: Take roots of positive algebraic factors and add, subtract or multiply fractional exponents exactly.

sections.title: Which part of a fractional index tells me the root?
sections.label: Root first, then raise
sections.intro: Read the denominator of the index as the order of the root. Read the numerator as the power. With positive bases, taking the root first often makes the arithmetic shorter.

blocks.html: For \(x>0\), \(x^{\frac{m}{n}}=(\sqrt[n]{x})^m\). If the base is a positive product, the root and the power act on all its factors.

figure.alt: A flow chart starts with a root, then shows a power and an optional reciprocal for a negative exponent.
figure.caption: The denominator gives the root. The numerator gives the power. A leading minus means take the final reciprocal.

blocks.title: Take a root of an algebraic power
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(27x^{9}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
blocks.hint: Take the root of both factors before applying the numerator as a power.
blocks.solution:
The root of order \(3\) gives \(3x^{3}\). This uses the positive value of \(x\).

Raise both of those factors to \(2\), giving coefficient \(9\) and index \(6\).

The simplified expression is \(9x^{6}\). In the requested form, \(c=9\), \(p=6\).

blocks.html: The square root of an arbitrary square is its non-negative magnitude. For a letter known to be positive, \(\sqrt{x^2}=x\).

blocks.title: Write a radical as a power of its base
blocks.prompt: For \(x>0\), Write \(\sqrt[3]{x}\times x^{3}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).
blocks.hint: The order of the root is the denominator of its fractional index.
blocks.solution:
Rewrite the radical as \(x^{\frac{1}{3}}\).

Add the indices using \(\frac{1}{3}+3=\frac{10}{3}\).

The result is \(x^{\frac{10}{3}}\), so \(p=\frac{10}{3}\).

blocks.html: When the base contains a coefficient and a power of a letter, show the root of each factor separately.

sections.title: How do I combine fractional indices with the same base?
sections.label: Add or subtract indices as exact fractions
sections.intro: The index laws for multiplication and division still apply to positive bases when the indices are fractions. Each arithmetic operation is performed on the indices.

blocks.html: Use a common denominator for addition and subtraction. For example, \(\frac{x^{\frac34}}{x^{-\frac12}}=x^{\frac54}\) since \(\frac34-(-\frac12)=\frac54\).

blocks.title: Add fractional indices with the same base
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(3x^{\frac{1}{3}}\times 4x^{\frac{4}{3}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
blocks.hint: Multiply the coefficients and add the fractional indices.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the numerical coefficients to get \(12\).

Use a common denominator to add the two indices: \(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{4}{3}=\frac{5}{3}\).

The simplified expression is \(12x^{\frac{5}{3}}\). In the requested form, \(c=12\), \(p=\frac{5}{3}\).

blocks.html: Subtract the entire denominator exponent, including its sign. A number outside a power is a coefficient and is treated separately.

blocks.title: Subtract a negative fractional index
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{4x^{\frac{1}{3}}}{3x^{-\frac{3}{4}}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
blocks.hint: Keep the negative index inside brackets when subtracting it.
blocks.solution:
Divide the coefficients to get \(\frac{4}{3}\).

Subtract the entire negative index: \(\frac{1}{3}-\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)=\frac{13}{12}\).

The simplified expression is \(\frac{4}{3}x^{\frac{13}{12}}\). In the requested form, \(c=\frac{4}{3}\), \(p=\frac{13}{12}\).

blocks.html: Write fractional indices on one line of arithmetic before putting the result above the base.

sections.title: How do I use a negative fractional index?
sections.label: Take a reciprocal of the positive power
sections.intro: First find the corresponding positive fractional power. A negative fractional power is its reciprocal, provided the base is positive.

blocks.html: When the power acts on a product, use the positive root and power on each factor. Take the reciprocal of the complete result.

blocks.title: Use a reciprocal after taking the root
blocks.prompt: For \(x>0\), write \(\left(27x^{9}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\) as \(\frac{1}{cx^{p}}\) with \(c>0\) and \(p>0\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
blocks.hint: Work out the positive power first and then invert the entire result.
blocks.solution:
The positive exponent of the same size gives \(9x^{6}\). Take the root of order \(3\) before raising to \(2\).

The original index is negative. Take the reciprocal of the whole result to obtain \(\frac{1}{9x^{6}}\).

blocks.html: The minus sign on an index changes which side of a fraction holds the factor. It does not make the base or the result negative.

blocks.title: Apply a fractional power to separate factors
blocks.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(16x^{6}y^{10}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\) as \(cx^{p}y^{q}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\).
blocks.hint: The outside square root applies to the coefficient and to both positive letter factors.
blocks.solution:
The index \(\frac{1}{2}\) asks for the positive square root.

Take the square root of each factor. Halve both letter indices, since both letters are positive.

The simplified expression is \(4x^{3}y^{5}\). In the requested form, \(c=4\), \(p=3\), \(q=5\).

blocks.html: Keep the exact fraction and use positive powers in the final expression if the question asks for them.

examples.title: Take a root of an algebraic power
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(4x^{4}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
solution: The root of order \(2\) gives \(2x^{2}\). This uses the positive value of \(x\).
Raise both of those factors to \(3\), giving coefficient \(8\) and index \(6\).
The simplified expression is \(8x^{6}\). In the requested form, \(c=8\), \(p=6\).

examples.title: Write a radical as a power of its base
examples.question: For \(x>0\), Write \(\sqrt{x}\times x^{2}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).
solution: Rewrite the radical as \(x^{\frac{1}{2}}\).
Add the indices using \(\frac{1}{2}+2=\frac{5}{2}\).
The result is \(x^{\frac{5}{2}}\), so \(p=\frac{5}{2}\).

examples.title: Add fractional indices with the same base
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(2x^{\frac{1}{2}}\times 3x^{\frac{3}{2}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
solution: Multiply the numerical coefficients to get \(6\).
Use a common denominator to add the two indices: \(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=2\).
The simplified expression is \(6x^{2}\). In the requested form, \(c=6\), \(p=2\).

examples.title: Subtract a negative fractional index
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{3x^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2x^{-\frac{2}{3}}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
solution: Divide the coefficients to get \(\frac{3}{2}\).
Subtract the entire negative index: \(\frac{1}{2}-\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)=\frac{7}{6}\).
The simplified expression is \(\frac{3}{2}x^{\frac{7}{6}}\). In the requested form, \(c=\frac{3}{2}\), \(p=\frac{7}{6}\).

examples.title: Use a reciprocal after taking the root
examples.question: For \(x>0\), write \(\left(4x^{4}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}}\) as \(\frac{1}{cx^{p}}\) with \(c>0\) and \(p>0\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
solution: The positive exponent of the same size gives \(8x^{6}\). Take the root of order \(2\) before raising to \(3\).
The original index is negative. Take the reciprocal of the whole result to obtain \(\frac{1}{8x^{6}}\).

examples.title: Apply a fractional power to separate factors
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(9x^{4}y^{8}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\) as \(cx^{p}y^{q}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\).
solution: The index \(\frac{1}{2}\) asks for the positive square root.
Take the square root of each factor. Halve both letter indices, since both letters are positive.
The simplified expression is \(3x^{2}y^{4}\). In the requested form, \(c=3\), \(p=2\), \(q=4\).

extraPractice.title: Take a root of an algebraic power
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(256x^{16}\right)^{\frac{3}{4}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
extraPractice.hint: Take the root of both factors before applying the numerator as a power.
extraPractice.solution:
The root of order \(4\) gives \(4x^{4}\). This uses the positive value of \(x\).

Raise both of those factors to \(3\), giving coefficient \(64\) and index \(12\).

The simplified expression is \(64x^{12}\). In the requested form, \(c=64\), \(p=12\).

extraPractice.title: Write a radical as a power of its base
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x>0\), Write \(\sqrt[4]{x}\times x^{4}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).
extraPractice.hint: The order of the root is the denominator of its fractional index.
extraPractice.solution:
Rewrite the radical as \(x^{\frac{1}{4}}\).

Add the indices using \(\frac{1}{4}+4=\frac{17}{4}\).

The result is \(x^{\frac{17}{4}}\), so \(p=\frac{17}{4}\).

extraPractice.title: Add fractional indices with the same base
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(4x^{\frac{1}{4}}\times 5x^{\frac{5}{4}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
extraPractice.hint: Multiply the coefficients and add the fractional indices.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiply the numerical coefficients to get \(20\).

Use a common denominator to add the two indices: \(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{5}{4}=\frac{3}{2}\).

The simplified expression is \(20x^{\frac{3}{2}}\). In the requested form, \(c=20\), \(p=\frac{3}{2}\).

extraPractice.title: Subtract a negative fractional index
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\frac{5x^{\frac{1}{4}}}{4x^{-\frac{4}{5}}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
extraPractice.hint: Keep the negative index inside brackets when subtracting it.
extraPractice.solution:
Divide the coefficients to get \(\frac{5}{4}\).

Subtract the entire negative index: \(\frac{1}{4}-\left(-\frac{4}{5}\right)=\frac{21}{20}\).

The simplified expression is \(\frac{5}{4}x^{\frac{21}{20}}\). In the requested form, \(c=\frac{5}{4}\), \(p=\frac{21}{20}\).

extraPractice.title: Use a reciprocal after taking the root
extraPractice.prompt: For \(x>0\), write \(\left(256x^{16}\right)^{-\frac{3}{4}}\) as \(\frac{1}{cx^{p}}\) with \(c>0\) and \(p>0\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
extraPractice.hint: Work out the positive power first and then invert the entire result.
extraPractice.solution:
The positive exponent of the same size gives \(64x^{12}\). Take the root of order \(4\) before raising to \(3\).

The original index is negative. Take the reciprocal of the whole result to obtain \(\frac{1}{64x^{12}}\).

extraPractice.title: Apply a fractional power to separate factors
extraPractice.prompt: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(25x^{8}y^{12}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\) as \(cx^{p}y^{q}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\).
extraPractice.hint: The outside square root applies to the coefficient and to both positive letter factors.
extraPractice.solution:
The index \(\frac{1}{2}\) asks for the positive square root.

Take the square root of each factor. Halve both letter indices, since both letters are positive.

The simplified expression is \(5x^{4}y^{6}\). In the requested form, \(c=5\), \(p=4\), \(q=6\).

glossary.definition: An exponent written as a fraction.
The denominator of a fractional index in lowest terms.
The non-negative square root.
A shared denominator used to combine fractions.
A base greater than zero.

revision.body:
Root first, then raise

For \(x>0\), \(x^{\frac{m}{n}}=(\sqrt[n]{x})^m\). If the base is a positive product, the root and the power act on all its factors.

Add or subtract indices as exact fractions

Use a common denominator for addition and subtraction. For example, \(\frac{x^{\frac34}}{x^{-\frac12}}=x^{\frac54}\) since \(\frac34-(-\frac12)=\frac54\).

Take a reciprocal of the positive power

When the power acts on a product, use the positive root and power on each factor. Take the reciprocal of the complete result.

Example

\((27x^6)^{\frac23}\) first becomes \((3x^2)^2\) after taking the cube root. The final result is \(9x^4\).

Check yourself

  • Simplify \((49a^4)^{\frac12}\) for \(a>0\).
  • Simplify \((16b^8)^{-\frac34}\) for \(b>0\).

Answers \(7a^2\) and \(\frac{1}{8b^6}\).

• The square root of an arbitrary square is its non-negative magnitude. For a letter known to be positive, \(\sqrt{x^2}=x\).
  • Subtract the entire denominator exponent, including its sign. A number outside a power is a coefficient and is treated separately.
  • The minus sign on an index changes which side of a fraction holds the factor. It does not make the base or the result negative.
revision.examTip: Keep the exact fraction and use positive powers in the final expression if the question asks for them.

igcse-0580-indices-ii-common-base-equati.description: Rewrite different bases using one common base, then solve the linear equation in the two indices.

sections.title: How do I rewrite a larger base?
sections.label: Find a common base greater than one
sections.intro: If one base is a positive integer power of the other, use the smaller base. Sometimes both displayed bases are powers of a still smaller number.

blocks.html: When rewriting \((a^m)^{kx+d}\), multiply the whole index by \(m\). Write \(a^{m(kx+d)}\) before expanding or matching the indices.

figure.alt: Arrows from the original left and right bases meet at the common base before finding the unknown.
figure.caption: Both sides reach the same base. Their exponents can then be compared directly.

blocks.title: Compare an unknown index with a fractional power
blocks.hint: Replace the larger base with a power of the smaller one.
blocks.solution:
Rewrite the base on the left as \(3^{3}\), so the left-hand index over base \(3\) is \(3x\).

The indices must match. Solve \(3x=2\).

The solution is \(x=\frac{2}{3}\).

blocks.html: Each term of an index bracket is multiplied. Rewriting the base can change both the coefficient of \(x\) and the constant term.

blocks.title: Equate two expressions in the exponent
blocks.hint: Multiply the entire bracket in the exponent when rewriting the right-hand base.
blocks.solution:
Replace \(27\) by \(3^{3}\). The whole right index is then \(3\left(x+2\right)\).

Equate indices. Collect the terms in \(x\) to obtain \(2x=2\).

The solution is \(x=1\).

blocks.html: Use a check by substitution, especially when the index found is a fraction or negative.

sections.title: What if one base is a reciprocal?
sections.label: Change to a negative power of the common base
sections.intro: A reciprocal of the chosen base is its exponent minus one. Raising that reciprocal to an unknown power multiplies the new exponent by minus one.

blocks.html: With \(a>1\), \(\left(\frac1a\right)^{x+d}=a^{-(x+d)}\). If there are several terms in the exponent, the minus sign applies to the entire group.

blocks.title: Use a reciprocal base before matching indices
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{x}=4^{3x+3}\).
blocks.hint: Rewrite a reciprocal base as the same base raised to minus one.
blocks.solution:
The reciprocal base is \(4^{-1}\). Raising it to \(x\) gives \(4^{-x}\).

Set \(-x=3x+3\). Rearrange to \(4x=-3\).

The solution is \(x=-\frac{3}{4}\).

blocks.html: A reciprocal base is not a negative base. Its value stays positive, but its rewritten index changes sign.

blocks.title: Combine powers before comparing the two sides
blocks.hint: Rewrite the larger base first. Then use the product law.
blocks.solution:
The first factor on the left is \(3^{3x}\). The product gives \(3^{3x+2}\).

Equate the two indices and rearrange to \(2x=2\).

The solution is \(x=1\).

blocks.html: Put brackets around an expression before applying a multiplier or a leading minus.

sections.title: What if both sides still have an unknown?
sections.label: Combine factors and solve a linear equation
sections.intro: After expressing all factors with the same base, combine each side into a single power. Only then compare the indices.

blocks.html: Move the unknown terms to one side and the constants to the other. Be prepared for a zero, negative or fractional answer.

blocks.title: Handle a quotient and a negative coefficient of x
blocks.hint: Subtract the denominator index from the full numerator index.
blocks.solution:
Rewrite the numerator as \(3^{3x}\). Subtract the denominator index \(2\).

The resulting index equation is \(3x-2=-x+3\). Collect the two terms that contain \(x\).

The solution is \(x=\frac{5}{4}\).

blocks.html: Do not equate indices while the displayed bases are different. Check that both sides have the same base after any products or quotients are simplified.

blocks.title: Find a common base for two larger bases
blocks.hint: A base that works for both sides can be smaller than either displayed base.
blocks.solution:
Use the common base \(3\). Both rewritten indices are products of an integer and an entire bracket.

Equate \(3\left(x+3\right)\) and \(4\left(x+2\right)\). Expanding and rearranging gives \(1x=1\).

The solution is \(x=1\).

blocks.html: These examples can all be rewritten to one base. Show that rewrite and the linear equation it produces.

examples.title: Compare an unknown index with a fractional power
examples.question: Solve \(4^{x}=2^{1}\).
solution: Rewrite the base on the left as \(2^{2}\), so the left-hand index over base \(2\) is \(2x\).
The indices must match. Solve \(2x=1\).
The solution is \(x=\frac{1}{2}\).

examples.title: Equate two expressions in the exponent
examples.question: Solve \(2^{3x+3}=4^{x+1}\).
solution: Replace \(4\) by \(2^{2}\). The whole right index is then \(2\left(x+1\right)\).
Equate indices. Collect the terms in \(x\) to obtain \(1x=-1\).
The solution is \(x=-1\).

examples.title: Use a reciprocal base before matching indices
examples.question: Solve \(\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{x}=3^{2x+2}\).
solution: The reciprocal base is \(3^{-1}\). Raising it to \(x\) gives \(3^{-x}\).
Set \(-x=2x+2\). Rearrange to \(3x=-2\).
The solution is \(x=-\frac{2}{3}\).

examples.title: Combine powers before comparing the two sides
examples.question: Solve \(4^{x}\times 2^{1}=2^{x+3}\).
solution: The first factor on the left is \(2^{2x}\). The product gives \(2^{2x+1}\).
Equate the two indices and rearrange to \(1x=2\).
The solution is \(x=2\).

examples.title: Handle a quotient and a negative coefficient of x
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{4^{x}}{2^{1}}=2^{-x+2}\).
solution: Rewrite the numerator as \(2^{2x}\). Subtract the denominator index \(1\).
The resulting index equation is \(2x-1=-x+2\). Collect the two terms that contain \(x\).
The solution is \(x=1\).

examples.title: Find a common base for two larger bases
examples.question: Solve \(4^{x+2}=8^{x+1}\).
solution: Use the common base \(2\). Both rewritten indices are products of an integer and an entire bracket.
Equate \(2\left(x+2\right)\) and \(3\left(x+1\right)\). Expanding and rearranging gives \(1x=1\).
The solution is \(x=1\).

extraPractice.title: Compare an unknown index with a fractional power
extraPractice.hint: Replace the larger base with a power of the smaller one.
extraPractice.solution:
Rewrite the base on the left as \(4^{4}\), so the left-hand index over base \(4\) is \(4x\).

The indices must match. Solve \(4x=3\).

The solution is \(x=\frac{3}{4}\).

extraPractice.title: Equate two expressions in the exponent
extraPractice.hint: Multiply the entire bracket in the exponent when rewriting the right-hand base.
extraPractice.solution:
Replace \(256\) by \(4^{4}\). The whole right index is then \(4\left(x+3\right)\).

Equate indices. Collect the terms in \(x\) to obtain \(1x=7\).

The solution is \(x=7\).

extraPractice.title: Use a reciprocal base before matching indices
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^{x}=5^{4x+4}\).
extraPractice.hint: Rewrite a reciprocal base as the same base raised to minus one.
extraPractice.solution:
The reciprocal base is \(5^{-1}\). Raising it to \(x\) gives \(5^{-x}\).

Set \(-x=4x+4\). Rearrange to \(5x=-4\).

The solution is \(x=-\frac{4}{5}\).

extraPractice.title: Combine powers before comparing the two sides
extraPractice.hint: Rewrite the larger base first. Then use the product law.
extraPractice.solution:
The first factor on the left is \(4^{4x}\). The product gives \(4^{4x+3}\).

Equate the two indices and rearrange to \(3x=2\).

The solution is \(x=\frac{2}{3}\).

extraPractice.title: Handle a quotient and a negative coefficient of x
extraPractice.hint: Subtract the denominator index from the full numerator index.
extraPractice.solution:
Rewrite the numerator as \(4^{4x}\). Subtract the denominator index \(3\).

The resulting index equation is \(4x-3=-x+4\). Collect the two terms that contain \(x\).

The solution is \(x=\frac{7}{5}\).

extraPractice.title: Find a common base for two larger bases
extraPractice.hint: A base that works for both sides can be smaller than either displayed base.
extraPractice.solution:
Use the common base \(4\). Both rewritten indices are products of an integer and an entire bracket.

Equate \(2\left(x+4\right)\) and \(3\left(x+3\right)\). Expanding and rearranging gives \(1x=-1\).

The solution is \(x=-1\).

glossary.definition: An equation with the unknown in an exponent.
An equation with the same solutions.
One divided by the original nonzero base.
An equation in which the unknown appears only to the first power after simplification.
A value that satisfies the original equation without rounding.

revision.body:
Find a common base greater than one

When rewriting \((a^m)^{kx+d}\), multiply the whole index by \(m\). Write \(a^{m(kx+d)}\) before expanding or matching the indices.

Change to a negative power of the common base

With \(a>1\), \(\left(\frac1a\right)^{x+d}=a^{-(x+d)}\). If there are several terms in the exponent, the minus sign applies to the entire group.

Combine factors and solve a linear equation

Move the unknown terms to one side and the constants to the other. Be prepared for a zero, negative or fractional answer.

Example

\(8^{x+1}=4^{2x}\) gives \(2^{3(x+1)}=2^{4x}\). Thus \(3x+3=4x\) and \(x=3\).

Check yourself

  • Solve \(25^x=5^3\).
  • Solve \(\left(\frac14\right)^x=4^{2x+6}\).

Answers \(x=\frac32\) and \(x=-2\).
revision.checks:
• Each term of an index bracket is multiplied. Rewriting the base can change both the coefficient of \(x\) and the constant term.
  • A reciprocal base is not a negative base. Its value stays positive, but its rewritten index changes sign.
  • Do not equate indices while the displayed bases are different. Check that both sides have the same base after any products or quotients are simplified.
revision.examTip: These examples can all be rewritten to one base. Show that rewrite and the linear equation it produces.
